text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Conditional Probability and the Reduced Sample Space",
    "scope": "Teaches the mathematical foundation of updating probabilities given prior knowledge. Explains how conditioning on an event alters the underlying universe by collapsing the sample space to a restricted subspace and renormalizing probabilities. Clarifies the formal definition, the non-commutativity of conditioning, and why conditioning on null events is undefined.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: $P(B|A) = \\frac{P(A \\cap B)}{P(A)}$ provided $P(A) > 0$",
      "Conditioning on impossible events ($P(A) = 0$) is mathematically undefined",
      "Concept of reduced sample space: outcomes outside $A$ receive zero probability mass, and $P(A)$ acts as the normalizing constant",
      "Directionality and non-commutativity: $P(B|A) \\neq P(A|B)$ in general due to differing reference denominators",
      "Distinction between joint probability $P(A \\cap B)$ and conditional probability $P(B|A)$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Independence of Two Events",
    "scope": "Introduces statistical independence between two events and contrasts it with causal or temporal relationships. Establishes both the conditional definition and the equivalent symmetric multiplicative definition. Highlights the critical difference between independent events and mutually exclusive (disjoint) events.",
    "key_points": [
      "Conditional definition: $A$ and $B$ are independent iff $P(B|A) = P(B)$ or $P(A|B) = P(A)$",
      "Multiplication theorem for independence: $A$ and $B$ are independent iff $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$",
      "Information-theoretic interpretation: knowledge of $A$'s occurrence yields zero update to the probability of $B$",
      "Independence vs. mutual exclusivity: two events with positive probabilities that are mutually exclusive ($A \\cap B = \\emptyset$) can never be independent because $P(A \\cap B) = 0 \\neq P(A)P(B)$",
      "Demonstration that events defined on the same physical trial (such as parity and divisibility on a single die roll) can be mathematically independent"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "The General Multiplication Rule and Chain Rule",
    "scope": "Extends conditional probability to compute the probability of intersections of events without assuming independence. Derives the general two-event product rule and generalizes it inductively to the chain rule for $k$ events. Explores sequential experiments such as sampling without replacement where event probabilities evolve dynamically.",
    "key_points": [
      "General two-event multiplication theorem: $P(A \\cap B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B)$",
      "Commutativity of set intersection: $A \\cap B = B \\cap A$ implies equivalence regardless of event labeling",
      "Chain rule for $k$ events: $P(A_1 \\cap A_2 \\cap \\dots \\cap A_k) = P(A_1)P(A_2|A_1)P(A_3|A_1 \\cap A_2) \\dots P(A_k|A_1 \\cap \\dots \\cap A_{k-1})$",
      "Simplification under independence: when all $A_i$ are independent, the chain rule reduces to the direct product $P(\\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i) = \\prod_{i=1}^k P(A_i)$",
      "Sequential modeling of dependent trials (e.g., drawing items without replacement)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "Mutual Independence of Multiple Events",
    "scope": "Addresses the subtleties of extending independence to collections of three or more events. Demonstrates why pairwise independence or a single joint product equality fails to guarantee mutual independence through formal counterexamples. Defines the complete combinatorial criteria required for mutual independence.",
    "key_points": [
      "Insufficiency of the 3-way product condition $P(A \\cap B \\cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C)$ (e.g., choosing $A = B$ and $C = \\emptyset$ satisfies the product formula but $A$ and $B$ remain dependent)",
      "Insufficiency of pairwise independence: events can be pairwise independent without being collectively independent",
      "Formal definition of mutual independence: a collection $\{A_1, \\dots, A_n\}$ is mutually independent iff for every sub-collection $\{A_{i_1}, \\dots, A_{i_k}\}$ with $2 \\le k \\le n$, $P(A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap A_{i_k}) = P(A_{i_1}) \\dots P(A_{i_k})$",
      "Total number of simultaneous equations required for $n$ events: $\\sum_{k=2}^n \\binom{n}{k} = 2^n - n - 1$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "The Law of Total Probability",
    "scope": "Formulates the partition-based decomposition of sample spaces to compute marginal probabilities of complex events. Proves that any event can be expressed as a union of mutually disjoint slices formed by intersecting with a partition. Establishes the standard computational framework for multi-stage processes and conditioning on unobserved intermediate states.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of a sample space partition: a collection $\{B_1, \\dots, B_k\}$ such that $\\bigcup_{i=1}^k B_i = S$, $B_i \\cap B_j = \\emptyset$ for $i \\neq j$, and $P(B_i) > 0$",
      "Set-theoretic decomposition: $A = (B_1 \\cap A) \\cup (B_2 \\cap A) \\cup \\dots \\cup (B_k \\cap A)$ where all terms are pairwise disjoint",
      "Formula for the Law of Total Probability: $P(A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i \\cap A) = \\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i)P(A|B_i)$",
      "Formal proof using countable additivity of probability measures across disjoint unions",
      "Application to multi-stage paths and compound transfer problems"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Bayes' Rule and Bayesian Updating",
    "scope": "Derives Bayes' Rule as the foundational mechanism for statistical inference and probability inversion. Explains the transition from prior probabilities of competing hypotheses to posterior probabilities after observing evidence. Breaks down the algebraic structure of the formula into prior probabilities, likelihoods, and normalizing marginal evidence.",
    "key_points": [
      "Statement of Bayes' Rule: $P(B_r|A) = \\frac{P(B_r \\cap A)}{P(A)} = \\frac{P(B_r)P(A|B_r)}{\\sum_{i=1}^k P(B_i)P(A|B_i)}$ for any partition state $B_r$",
      "Formal proof combining conditional probability with the Law of Total Probability in the denominator",
      "Terminology: prior probability $P(B_r)$, likelihood $P(A|B_r)$, marginal evidence $P(A)$, and posterior probability $P(B_r|A)$",
      "Conceptual role: inverting conditional statements to reason from observed effects back to latent causes"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Random Variables and Sample Space Classification",
    "scope": "Establishes the definition of a random variable as a deterministic function mapping sample space outcomes to the real number line. Differentiates between discrete and continuous sample spaces based on cardinality. Formalizes notation conventions and explains how numerical values induce event preimages in the sample space.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: a random variable $X$ is a function $X: S \\to \\mathbb{R}$ assigning a real number $x$ to each outcome $\\omega \\in S$",
      "Notation: uppercase letter $X$ denotes the random variable (the function), lowercase $x$ denotes a specific realized value",
      "Event preimage: the notation $\{X = x\}$ denotes the subset of outcomes $\{\\omega \\in S : X(\\omega) = x\}$",
      "Classification of sample spaces: discrete (finite or countably infinite elements) versus continuous (uncountably infinite elements, such as intervals on the real line $[0, \\infty)$)",
      "Indicator/Bernoulli random variables: mapping binary qualitative states (e.g., defective vs. non-defective) to $\{0, 1\}$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "Discrete Probability Distributions and Probability Mass Functions",
    "scope": "Defines probability distributions for discrete random variables via the probability mass function (PMF). Details the axiomatic requirements that guarantee mathematical validity of any discrete distribution. Examines standard tabular and functional models, including the derivation of the hypergeometric distribution for finite population sampling without replacement.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of Probability Mass Function (PMF): $f(x) = P(X = x)$",
      "Axiomatic conditions of a valid PMF: (1) $f(x) \\ge 0$ for all $x$, and (2) $\\sum_x f(x) = 1$",
      "Evaluation of discrete event probabilities: $P(X \\in E) = \\sum_{x \\in E} f(x)$",
      "Hypergeometric distribution formulation for sampling $n$ items without replacement from population $N$ with $K$ successes: $P(X = x) = \\frac{\\binom{K}{x}\\binom{N - K}{n - x}}{\\binom{N}{n}}$",
      "Support and boundary constraints on hypergeometric parameters: $\\max(0, n - (N - K)) \\le x \\le \\min(K, n)$"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "The Cumulative Distribution Function for Discrete Variables",
    "scope": "Introduces the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) as an alternative complete specification of a random variable's probability law. Explains the step-function structure of discrete CDFs, right-continuity, and jump discontinuities at support points. Teaches how to compute interval probabilities directly from the CDF and convert back and forth between PMF and CDF.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of Cumulative Distribution Function: $F(x) = P(X \\le x) = \\sum_{t \\le x} f(t)$ for all $-\\infty < x < \\infty$",
      "Structural properties: $F(x)$ is non-decreasing, defined on all of $\\mathbb{R}$, and right-continuous with jump discontinuities at discrete support points",
      "Jump magnitude relationship: the jump height at any point $x_k$ equals the probability mass $f(x_k) = F(x_k) - \\lim_{x \\to x_k^-} F(x)$",
      "Asymptotic limits: $\\lim_{x \\to -\\infty} F(x) = 0$ and $\\lim_{x \\to \\infty} F(x) = 1$",
      "Interval probability identities: $P(a < X \\le b) = F(b) - F(a)$ and $P(X > x) = 1 - F(x)$"
    ]
  }
]
